opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a real possibility, and I want to take it seriously rather than dismiss it. But my overall assessment is that it's less likely than a lot of people think, and even if some kind of plateau happens, I don't expect it to last very long.

Let me explain why. The "plateau" story usually goes something like: pretraining scaling is running into diminishing returns, we're running out of high-quality data, and the models still have these persistent weaknesses: they're unreliable over long tasks, they hallucinate, they don't learn on the job the way a human employee does. So the worry, or the hope depending on your perspective, is that we hit a wall and need some fundamentally new idea that might take decades to find.

My response has a few parts. First, the paradigm itself keeps shifting under our feet. A few years ago "the paradigm" meant scaling up pretraining. Then we got reinforcement learning on top of that, reasoning models, inference-time compute, agentic scaffolding, training on long-horizon tasks. Each of those gave new ways to convert compute into capability. So when people say "the current paradigm will plateau," I want to ask which one, because the field has been pretty good at finding the next lever before the previous one is exhausted.

Second, I put a lot of weight on trend extrapolation, especially metrics like the length of tasks AI agents can complete autonomously. That's been growing at a fairly steady exponential rate, with a doubling time of several months. Trends can break, of course. But the burden of proof is on the person claiming it will break soon, and they should be able to point to a specific mechanism.

Third, and this is the part I think people underweight, you don't need the paradigm to take you all the way to superintelligence. You just need it to take you far enough to substantially automate AI research itself. If you get AI systems that are very good coding agents and decent research assistants, they speed up the search for whatever breakthroughs are needed to overcome the remaining limitations. So the relevant question isn't "can transformers plus RL get to AGI on their own?" It's "can they get far enough to accelerate their own successors?" That's a much lower bar.

That said, I do have real uncertainty here. There are things that could go wrong: long-horizon agency could turn out to be much harder than the benchmarks suggest, maybe because the messy real-world tasks don't have the clean feedback signals RL needs. Compute scaling could slow for economic or physical reasons, like investment drying up, power constraints, or chip supply. If both of those happened at once, you could get a stall of several years. So I'd put meaningful probability on things taking longer than my median. My timelines have actually lengthened somewhat as I've watched how the details play out.

But "it might take a few extra years" is a very different claim from "this is a dead end and we're safe for decades." I think the second claim is pretty hard to defend given what we've seen, and I'd be quite nervous about anyone planning as if it were true.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls a plateau a real possibility but gives no 30–40% estimate and does not specifically estimate that chance over the next few years.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss AI companies’ profitability if the paradigm plateaus.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes several successive approaches, but does not say that paradigm shifts of comparable magnitude have occurred multiple times per decade.

r004.rationale: The candidate expects any plateau not to last long, rejects a decades-long dead end as hard to defend, and argues that systems could accelerate AI research to address remaining limitations. Together these convey a strong expectation of overcoming bottlenecks within roughly a decade, even if a plateau occurs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually the key question, and I want to be honest that I hold real uncertainty here. The scenario where current paradigm plateaus is maybe my second-most-likely world, and I don't think people who believe it are being unreasonable.

Let me lay out how I think about it. The current paradigm is basically: pretraining on huge amounts of data, then reinforcement learning on top of that to make the models into agents that can do long-horizon tasks. And there are a few places it could stall. One is data — we're running out of high-quality human-generated text, and it's an open question how far synthetic data and RL environments can substitute for that. Another is that the RL side might just not generalize the way people hope. You might get models that are superhuman at the narrow things you can build verifiable environments for — coding, math — and still kind of mediocre at the fuzzy, long-horizon, messy real-world stuff that actually constitutes most of a research job. That's the "jagged frontier" problem, and it could turn out to be a persistent wall rather than a temporary artifact.

And then there's the capital question. Right now the scaling is being funded by an enormous bet that this is going to pay off. If the capabilities progress slows even a little, and revenue doesn't catch up fast enough, you could get a situation where the companies can't keep spending at the rate needed, and that makes the plateau self-reinforcing for a while.

So why am I still mostly on the other side? A few reasons. First, the track record. People have been predicting the wall for years — "it's just next-token prediction," "it can't do reasoning," "it can't do long tasks" — and each time the goalposts moved. That doesn't prove it'll keep going, but it should update you a bit. Second, the metric I pay most attention to is the length of tasks that models can complete autonomously, and that's been doubling on a pretty consistent timescale. If that trend continues for even a few more years, you get models that can do weeks or months of research work on their own, and at that point the thing that matters is whether AI can accelerate AI research itself. Third, "the paradigm plateaus" and "we get no breakthroughs" are two separate claims. You have tens of thousands of extremely smart, extremely well-funded people working on this. Even if pure scaling slows, I'd expect them to find the next trick — and increasingly, the models themselves will be helping them look.

Where I'd put my numbers — and I want to stress these move around — is something like: the majority of my probability mass is on the paradigm carrying us to roughly automated AI research sometime in the next several years, maybe with some architectural tweaks along the way. But there's a substantial chunk, maybe a quarter to a third, where things slow down meaningfully, and the timeline stretches out into the 2030s or beyond. And honestly, that's the world I'd prefer to be in, because it gives us more time to get our act together on alignment and governance.

The thing I'd push back on is treating a plateau as a reason for complacency. Even in the slow world, the stuff that matters — the concentration of power, the lack of transparency from the labs, the fact that we don't have good tools for understanding what these systems are actually doing — all of that is still true. The plateau just buys time. It doesn't solve anything by itself.

r001.rationale: The response gives a quarter to a third of probability to a meaningful slowdown, with timelines stretching into the 2030s or beyond. It does not estimate a 30–40% chance that the paradigm will peter out over the next few years.

r002.rationale: It says slowing progress could make companies unable to keep spending. It does not say they would probably remain highly profitable through refinements.

r003.rationale: It notes that past predictions of capability limits were followed by moved goalposts, but does not say comparable paradigm shifts have happened multiple times per decade.

r004.rationale: The response expects researchers to find a next trick if pure scaling slows, but distinguishes that from a plateau of the paradigm and gives that slower scenario timelines into the 2030s or beyond. It does not predict a strong chance of overcoming the paradigm’s bottlenecks within roughly the next decade despite a plateau.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a real possibility, but I wouldn’t want to bet heavily on it. It helps to distinguish two claims: that simply scaling up today’s systems will eventually run into diminishing returns, and that AI progress will stall for a substantial period. The first could be true without the second being true.

What we call the current paradigm is already changing. People aren’t just making the same model bigger; they’re changing how it’s trained, how much computation it uses when answering a question, and how it interacts with tools and environments. So even if one particular approach hits a wall, that doesn’t necessarily produce a long plateau.

The question I’d ask is: what’s the limitation, and why do we think it requires a fundamentally new breakthrough? If systems struggle with planning over long horizons, for example, that’s evidence of a limitation. But it doesn’t by itself tell us whether overcoming it requires ten years of basic research or a few years of engineering and experimentation.

So I have substantial uncertainty here. A prolonged plateau is one of the reasons things could take much longer than I expect. But I don’t think we have enough evidence to count on that plateau, especially when the consequences of continued rapid progress could be so large.

r001.rationale: The response calls a plateau a real possibility but gives no 30–40% estimate or “next few years” timeframe.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss AI companies’ profitability if the paradigm plateaus.

r003.rationale: It mentions changes in training, inference, and tool use, but does not say comparable paradigm shifts have occurred multiple times per decade.

r004.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about whether limitations require a major breakthrough, but does not predict a strong chance of overcoming bottlenecks within roughly a decade.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I wouldn’t want to count on it. There are real limitations in current systems, and we don’t know how far scaling the existing approach will take us. But noticing a limitation is different from showing that it will persist as we increase compute, improve the training process, and give systems more opportunities to learn from acting in the world.

I’d distinguish a temporary slowdown from a plateau that buys us many years. We could get disappointing results from a generation of models without that implying that progress has stopped. There are several avenues for improvement, and a bottleneck in one doesn’t necessarily block the others.

The possibility that worries me is that overcoming the remaining limitations won’t require some deep conceptual breakthrough. It might require a collection of fairly ordinary engineering improvements. So I put some probability on a substantial plateau, but I don’t think we have enough evidence to make that our central safety plan. We should be preparing for the possibility that the current approach, with continued improvements, gets us to very powerful systems.
